The rubric has 21 criteria in three tiers, 12 of them core. Each criterion page gives the definition; when the criterion counts as met, partially met and not met; when the criterion is not applicable; its prerequisites; and the text evidence from the scoping review corpus.
The site is generated from rubric_draft_02.11.2026.xlsx.

title: Third-party certification
text:
NotePackages containing datasets that cannot be shared



This criterion is recommended in general. For packages that do not contain all datasets needed because some cannot be shared, it becomes a core criterion: without a third-party certification, only the Tier 1 criteria are assessed, so the package can get at most Bronze. With a certification, the core criteria that need the data are rated from the certificate, so Silver and Gold become possible. See rules 3 and 4 in Rules of the badge system.

The code runs to completion without any execution errors caused by the code itself (bugs). Errors from missing packages or file paths are scored under dependency resolution and path resolution.
Supported by: #80 and #100 ‘could not detect any coding errors’, #113 ‘the code ran error-free’, #23 workflowr only commits code that runs, #115 runnability as prerequisite.








WarningPartially met



The code stops with execution errors, but the reproducer can fix them with minor, unambiguous changes that require no analytical decision (e.g. installing a missing package, adjusting a file path or working directory, a syntax change due to a newer software version), within a stated time limit (e.g. one week). Each fix is documented and reported to the authors, and the fixed code runs to completion.

“Since not all generated code can be executed, the P_agent,i is set to 0 for the non-executable instances, resulting in a maximum performance gap of 1.0” (p.7, lines 21–22)

“If there were a change to the data or the code, re-weaving the source file would update the results and confirm the reproducibility of the analysis (or not, if there were some error in the code)” (p. 3)

“For curating, we attempted to fix mistakes in a team’s code only if the following two conditions were met: it had to be obvious that it was a mistake and, if so, that we could determine a counterfactual scenario of what the authors would have done instead had they become aware of the mistake. We only changed code when we did not have to make any decisions.” (p. 9, Methods — Curated section)


#131 Guide for Accelerating Computational Reproducibility in the Social Sciences · injunctive

Whenever code is available in the reproduction package, you should be able to debug those scripts. There are at least five types of debugging that can improve the reproduction package:
Code cleaning: Simplify the instructions (e.g., by wrapping repetitive steps in a function or a loop) or remove redundant code (i.e., old code that was commented out) while keeping the original output intact.
Performance improvement: Replace the original instructions with new ones that perform the same tasks but take less time (e.g., choose one numerical optimization algorithm over another while still obtaining the same results).
Adding unit tests: Add if/then statements after a code chunk or section (more or less every 100 lines of code) where you test that variables or statistics are computing as expected. If the value has changed, create a warning message that mentions what object has changed.
Environment set up: Modify the code to include correct paths to files, specific versions of software, and instructions to install missing packages or libraries.
Correcting errors: A coding error will occur when a section of the code in the production package executes a procedure that is in direct contradiction with the intended procedure expressed in the documentation (i.e., paper or code comments). For example, an error will occur if the paper specifies that the analysis is performed on a population of males, but the code restricts the analysis to females only..

“the reproduction analyst makes an error or did not spend enough time troubleshooting… If those are the sole reasons why the reproduction test failed, then the original outcome may have been reported precisely despite the independent failure to reproduce them.” (p.131)

title: Data deposit
text:
TipMet



The data required to reproduce the analysis are provided, preferably in a trusted repository with a persistent identifier (e.g. a DOI). These can be either the raw data or the cleaned (analysis) data; whether the matching cleaning code is present is scored under code deposit. If the data cannot be shared (e.g. proprietary or confidential data), the criterion is also met when the README (1) states why the data cannot be shared (e.g. license, data use agreement, privacy law), (2) documents completely how an independent researcher can obtain the same data, to the standard of data provenance (provider, version/vintage, application procedure, costs, waiting times), and (3) the authors commit to preserving the data for a stated period (e.g. at least five years) or have deposited them in a secure archive.
Supported by: #109 raw vs. analysis data both accepted, raw needs cleaning code (note), #131 L5 (analysis data) vs. L10 (raw + analysis), #12 ‘analytical data set is available’, #100 analysis data only, #132 raw + analysis + cleaning code, #93.








WarningPartially met



Some of the data required are missing: e.g. one of several data sources, the data behind some results (e.g. appendix tables), or only a subsample of the data used is provided. For data that cannot be shared: the reason is stated, but the access documentation is incomplete or there is no preservation commitment.
Supported by: Partial data: #131 L7 (raw data partially available), #15 ‘missing the data used for analysis’, #141 raw data missing.








ImportantNot met



No dataset is available, and for data that cannot be shared, neither the reason nor how to obtain the data is documented.
Supported by: #86 ‘no shared data’, #144 unavailability of data the main barrier, #98 rating 1, #131 L1/L2, #70 fail unless law prevents it.

Level 1 (L1): No data or code are available. Possible improvements include adding: raw data, analysis data, cleaning code, and analysis code. Level 2 (L2): Code scripts are available (partial or complete), but no data are available. Possible improvements include adding: raw data and analysis data.
Level 3 (L3): Analytic data and code are partially available, but raw data and cleaning code are missing. Possible improvements include: completing analysis data and/or code, adding raw data, and adding analysis code.
Level 4 (L4): All analytic data sets and analysis code are available, but the code fails to run or produces results inconsistent with the paper (not CRA). Possible improvements include: debugging the analysis code or obtaining raw data.
Level 5 (L5): Analytic data sets and analysis code are available and they produce the same results as presented in the paper (CRA). The reproducibility package may be improved by obtaining the original raw data.
Note: This is the highest level that most published research papers can attain currently. Computational reproducibility from raw data is required for papers that are reproducible at Level 6 and above.
Level 6 (L6): Cleaning code scripts are available (partial or complete), but raw data is missing. Possible improvements include: adding raw data.
Level 7 (L7): Cleaning code is available and complete, and raw data is partially available. Possible improvements: adding raw data.
Level 8 (L8): All the materials (raw data, analytic data, cleaning code, and analysis code) are available. However, the cleaning code fails to run or produces different results from those presented in the paper (not CRR) or the analysis code fails to run or produces results inconsistent with the paper (not CRA). Possible improvements: debugging the cleaning or analysis code.
Level 9 (L9): All the materials (raw data, analytic data, cleaning code, and analysis code) are available. The analysis code produces the same output as presented in the paper (CRA). However, the cleaning code fails to run or produces different results from those presented in the paper (not CRR). Possible improvements: debugging the cleaning code.
Level 10 (L10): All necessary materials are available and produce consistent results with those presented in the paper. The reproduction involves minimal effort and can be conducted starting from the analytic data ( CRA) and the raw data (CRR). Note that Level 10 is aspirational and may be unattainable for most research published today.

Note: Can be analytic or raw data. If raw data is submitted, then cleaning codes must be provided.

title: How to use the rubric
text:
Evidence on the criterion page

In the corpus
This section provides information regarding a criterion extracted from 145 papers in the scoping review, and covers:

Sources: the number of sources that mention the criterion.
Injunctive: the share of sources mentioning the criterion that frame it as a rule/requirement or a barrier to reproduce, using prescriptive or proscriptive languages.

key words: must, should, require, etc.
examples: “Authors must provide all data and code necessary to replicate all reported analyses”, “Code must execute without errors when run sequentially from the master script”, or “unavailable source codes is a critical barrier to reproduce results”

Descriptive: the share of sources mentioning the criterion that describe it as a common practice.

key words: most journals, most researchers, typically, common practice, widespread norms, etc.
examples: “Researchers typically include a master script to facilitate automated re-execution” or “Most CCS journals now expect replication packages to be deposited upon acceptance”

Tacit: inferred by the coder that the author(s) require(s) this criterion as a part of reproducibility check, but it is not stated explicitly as a rule.

example: a paper outlining a reproducibility attempt flagged hardcoded path errors during execution but doesn’t explicitly mention path resolution as a criterion.

Automatable: the share of sources mentioning the criterion, which state that it can be checked automatically.
Manual check: the share of sources mentioning the criterion, which state it should be verified manually.
Automation unclear: no clear information available in the text regarding the automation of that criterion.
LLM sources: among sources confirming automation potential (Automatable), how many of them do involve large language model.

Level 1 (L1): No data or code are available. Possible improvements include adding: raw data, analysis data, cleaning code, and analysis code. Level 2 (L2): Code scripts are available (partial or complete), but no data are available. Possible improvements include adding: raw data and analysis data.
Level 3 (L3): Analytic data and code are partially available, but raw data and cleaning code are missing. Possible improvements include: completing analysis data and/or code, adding raw data, and adding analysis code.
Level 4 (L4): All analytic data sets and analysis code are available, but the code fails to run or produces results inconsistent with the paper (not CRA). Possible improvements include: debugging the analysis code or obtaining raw data.
Level 5 (L5): Analytic data sets and analysis code are available and they produce the same results as presented in the paper (CRA). The reproducibility package may be improved by obtaining the original raw data.
Note: This is the highest level that most published research papers can attain currently. Computational reproducibility from raw data is required for papers that are reproducible at Level 6 and above.
Level 6 (L6): Cleaning code scripts are available (partial or complete), but raw data is missing. Possible improvements include: adding raw data.
Level 7 (L7): Cleaning code is available and complete, and raw data is partially available. Possible improvements: adding raw data.
Level 8 (L8): All the materials (raw data, analytic data, cleaning code, and analysis code) are available. However, the cleaning code fails to run or produces different results from those presented in the paper (not CRR) or the analysis code fails to run or produces results inconsistent with the paper (not CRA). Possible improvements: debugging the cleaning or analysis code.
Level 9 (L9): All the materials (raw data, analytic data, cleaning code, and analysis code) are available. The analysis code produces the same output as presented in the paper (CRA). However, the cleaning code fails to run or produces different results from those presented in the paper (not CRR). Possible improvements: debugging the cleaning code.
Level 10 (L10): All necessary materials are available and produce consistent results with those presented in the paper. The reproduction involves minimal effort and can be conducted starting from the analytic data ( CRA) and the raw data (CRR). Note that Level 10 is aspirational and may be unattainable for most research published today.

If the first reference to this data source is found on page 1 of the appendix, you should record its location as “A1”. Do this for all data sources mentioned in the paper. Each row represents a unique data source.
Data sources also vary by unit of analysis, with some sources matching the same unit of analysis used in the paper (as in previous examples). In contrast, others may be less clear, e.g., “our information on regional minimum wages comes from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.” You should record such data source as “regional minimum wages from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.”
Next, look at the reproduction package and map the data sources mentioned in the paper to the data files in the reproduction package. In the Location column, record their folder locations relative to the main reproduction folder1. In addition to looking at the existing data files, we recommend that you also review the first lines of all code files (especially cleaning code), looking for lines that call the datasets. Inspecting these scripts may help you understand how different data sources are used, and possibly identify any missing files from the reproduction package. Whenever a data source contains multiple files, enter them in the same cell, separated by semicolon (;).

title: Badge pipeline
text:
Rules of the badge system

In order to get a badge, a reproduction package must fully meet all applicable core criteria of that tier and of every lower tier.
Each reproduction package gets a summary of how many criteria (core and recommended) are met, partially met, not met, and not applicable, and a badge if rule 1 is met.
If not all input datasets are in the package and there is no third-party certification, only the Tier 1 criteria are assessed, so the package can get at most Bronze. The summary then covers only the Tier 1 criteria; findings on the other data-independent criteria can be reported as comments.
If not all input datasets are in the package but the package has third-party certification, the data-dependent, core criteria (path resolution, coding error handling, numerical output match, and table and figure match) are rated from the certificate or the signed letter.

A criterion is fully met only if the certificate or a signed letter, issued by an independent party, explicitly confirms it, e.g. that the code ran to completion (Silver) or that all results were reproduced (Gold).

title: Badge pipeline
text:
Order of checking
A reproduction package contains the manuscript, a README, the code (R or Stata) and a codebook (not needed if all data are generated by the code), plus, optionally, the datasets (included in the package, or deposited separately under a PID/DOI) and a log file (Stata). It is checked in four steps:

Data situation check. This sorts the package into one of four routes:

Route 1a: all datasets are generated by the code (not downloaded). All tiers are possible, and N/A conditions C1 and C2 apply.
Route 1b: all input datasets are in the package (included or under a PID/DOI). All tiers are possible, and N/A condition C2 applies.
Route 1c: not all input datasets are in the package, but there is third-party certification or a signed letter from an independent party. All tiers are possible.
Route 1d: not all input datasets are in the package, and there is no certification. The package can get at most Bronze.

Data-independent criteria check. These can be checked without the data being in the package:

core: documentation, data provenance, license, code deposit, data deposit, dependency resolution, computing environment, codes consistent with claims
recommended: artifacts longevity/sustainability, code annotation, workflow/reproduction tree, version control, commands logs traceability, test code coverage
two of these depend on the data situation. Code deposit: if only raw data are included, the cleaning code must be included too. Data deposit: if data cannot be shared, the reason, how to obtain full access, and a commitment to preserve the data must be documented.

Data-dependent criteria check. These can only be checked with the data, so this step depends on the route:

Step 3a (routes 1a and 1b): run the code and check the core criteria path resolution, coding error handling, numerical output match and table and figure match, and the recommended criteria code runs without manual intervention and dynamic code inspection.
Step 3b (route 1c): evaluate the four core criteria from the signed letter from independent reproducers or the certificate (rule 4). See third-party certification.
No Step 3 (route 1d): only the Tier 1 criteria are assessed (rule 3).

Award the badge. Apply rule 1:

No badge: not all applicable Tier 1 core criteria are fully met.
Bronze: all applicable Tier 1 core criteria are fully met, but the package is on route 1d or not all applicable Tier 2 core criteria are fully met.
Silver: all applicable Tier 1 and Tier 2 core criteria are fully met, but not all applicable Tier 3 core criteria.
Gold: all applicable core criteria of all three tiers are fully met.


Within criteria checks (step 2 and 3), always check criteria with a lower check order first. The number counts the prerequisite steps above a criterion (0 = no prerequisite coded, — = no prerequisite links coded at all). Each criterion page lists what it builds on and what it is a prerequisite for; the Dependency graph shows all links at once.
